# Communication Automation: Slack, Discord, Telegram, and Notion

##### The alert nobody reads

A startup wired up monitoring for their order pipeline. Every event posted to `#alerts`: every successful order, every retry, every warning, every failure. Within two weeks the channel was producing 400 messages a day. Within three weeks, everyone had muted it.

Then a payment integration broke. The failure alert fired correctly, on time, with a perfect stack trace — into a muted channel. Nobody noticed for eleven hours.

This is **notification fatigue**, and it is a well-documented phenomenon; research on interruption and attention (Iqbal & Horvitz, 2010) shows that frequent low-value notifications don't just get ignored, they measurably degrade people's ability to respond to the important ones. A large fraction of automation requests are fundamentally about communication — "tell the right person when X happens" — so the technical skill of *posting a message* is only half the job. The other half is judgment about **what, where, and how often**.

##### Slack: the workplace default

Slack is the platform you will automate most. There are two ways in.

**Incoming webhooks** are the simple path: you create one in Slack's app settings, get a URL bound to a single channel, and POST JSON to it. No OAuth, no tokens to refresh. Perfect for "post a notification" and nothing else.

```bash
curl -X POST "https://hooks.slack.com/services/T00/B00/XXXXXXXXXXXX" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "text": "New enterprise lead: Northwind Logistics",
        "blocks": [
          { "type": "header",
            "text": { "type": "plain_text", "text": "🚀 New Enterprise Lead" } },
          { "type": "section",
            "fields": [
              { "type": "mrkdwn", "text": "*Company:*\nNorthwind Logistics" },
              { "type": "mrkdwn", "text": "*Team size:*\n45" },
              { "type": "mrkdwn", "text": "*Contact:*\nAnanya Rao" },
              { "type": "mrkdwn", "text": "*Value:*\n₹4,50,000" }
            ] },
          { "type": "actions",
            "elements": [
              { "type": "button",
                "text": { "type": "plain_text", "text": "Open in CRM" },
                "url": "https://app.hubspot.com/contacts/12345",
                "style": "primary" }
            ] },
          { "type": "context",
            "elements": [ { "type": "mrkdwn", "text": "cc <@U024BE7LH> · via automation" } ] }
        ]
      }'
```

**The Slack API with a bot token** is the fuller path — needed for reading messages, listing channels, uploading files, adding reactions, or posting to any channel dynamically. You create a Slack app, grant scopes (`chat:write`, `files:write`, `channels:read`), install it to the workspace, and use the `xoxb-` bot token. Zapier, Make and n8n all wrap this behind an OAuth connection.

**Formatting matters more than beginners think.** Slack's `mrkdwn` is subtly different from standard Markdown: `*bold*` uses single asterisks, `_italic_` uses underscores, `~strike~`, and links are `<https://url|label>`. **Block Kit** — the `blocks` array above — is what separates a professional-looking notification from a wall of text. Slack's Block Kit Builder is an interactive playground where you design the JSON visually and paste the result into your automation.

**Mentions** need real IDs, not display names. `<@U024BE7LH>` pings a user; `<!here>` notifies active channel members; `<!channel>` notifies everyone (use sparingly — this is the button that makes people mute your channel). Typing `@ananya` as plain text does nothing at all; it just renders as characters.

##### Discord and Telegram

**Discord** is dominant in communities, gaming, crypto and increasingly among developer and student groups. Its webhook model is nearly identical to Slack's: create a webhook in channel settings, POST JSON. Discord's rich formatting uses **embeds**:

```json
{
  "content": "Deployment finished",
  "embeds": [{
    "title": "Build #482 succeeded",
    "description": "Deployed to production in 3m 12s",
    "color": 3066993,
    "fields": [
      { "name": "Branch", "value": "main", "inline": true },
      { "name": "Author", "value": "ananya", "inline": true }
    ],
    "footer": { "text": "CI pipeline" },
    "timestamp": "2026-03-14T09:12:44Z"
  }]
}
```

Discord's `color` is a decimal integer, not a hex string — `3066993` is green. That trips everyone up once.

**Telegram** is the best choice for personal and mobile-first alerts, and it is free with no seat limits — genuinely useful for Indian small businesses where the team already lives on their phones. Setup is charmingly simple: message `@BotFather`, run `/newbot`, receive a token. To send a message you need the chat ID, which you get by messaging your bot then calling `getUpdates`.

```bash
# 1. find your chat_id after sending your bot a message
curl "https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/getUpdates"

# 2. send a formatted message
curl -X POST "https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/sendMessage" \
  -d chat_id=987654321 \
  -d parse_mode=Markdown \
  -d text="*Order ORD-1042* received — ₹4,998 from Ananya Rao"
```

Telegram also supports inline keyboards (tappable buttons that call back into your automation), file sending, and group chats — making it a surprisingly capable interface for approval flows.

##### Interactive messages and mentions

Notifications that only inform are half a solution. **Interactive messages** let the recipient act without leaving chat.

In Slack, Block Kit `actions` blocks render buttons, dropdowns and date pickers. When someone clicks, Slack POSTs a payload to an **interactivity request URL** you configure — which can be an n8n Webhook node or a Make custom webhook. Your workflow reads which button was pressed and by whom, then acts.

The classic pattern is an approval flow:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Workflow
    participant S as Slack
    participant M as Manager
    participant A as Approval workflow
    W->>S: post request with Approve / Reject buttons
    S->>M: shows message in #approvals
    M->>S: clicks Approve
    S->>A: POST interaction payload to webhook
    A->>A: verify signature, record decision
    A->>S: update original message ("✅ Approved by Ravi")
    A->>W: continue the process
```

Two details make this production-grade: **verify Slack's request signature** (the `X-Slack-Signature` header) so nobody can forge approvals, and **update the original message** after action so it cannot be clicked twice.

Discord offers the equivalent through message components and interactions; Telegram through inline keyboards and callback queries.

##### Notion as structured storage

Notion is not a messaging tool, but it belongs in this day because it fills the gap chat leaves: **chat is ephemeral, Notion is durable**.

A Notion **database** is a structured table with typed properties — title, rich text, number, select, multi-select, date, person, checkbox, relation, formula. The API lets you create pages (rows), query with filters and sorts, and update properties.

Creating a page via the API means describing properties in Notion's specific shape:

```json
{
  "parent": { "database_id": "8f21c0de3b7a4c1991f26ad0e5b3c742" },
  "properties": {
    "Name":    { "title":  [{ "text": { "content": "Northwind Logistics" } }] },
    "Status":  { "select": { "name": "New" } },
    "Owner":   { "people": [{ "id": "b1e6c0d9-f731-4a52-9e10-7bd32f8c1a44" }] },
    "Value":   { "number": 450000 },
    "Contact": { "email":  "ananya@example.com" },
    "Created": { "date":   { "start": "2026-03-14" } }
  }
}
```

That nesting is verbose but logical — each property type has its own value shape, and mismatching them is the number one cause of Notion API errors. Note also that Notion's API is rate-limited to roughly three requests per second, so bulk operations need throttling.

Used together, the pattern is: **write the record to Notion, post the alert to Slack with a link to the Notion page.** The chat message is the interrupt; Notion is the memory.

##### Choosing notification channels wisely

Here is the framework the assignment asks for, and it is genuinely useful in client conversations.

| Information type | Channel | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Urgent, needs action now** (payment failed, system down, VIP lead) | Slack/Telegram DM or channel **with a mention** | Interrupt is justified; mention makes ownership explicit |
| **Important, needs action today** (new lead, approval request) | Slack channel, **no** `@channel` | Visible without interrupting everyone |
| **Routine, aggregate** (daily orders, weekly signups) | **One scheduled digest** — email or a morning Slack post | Batches 200 events into one readable message |
| **Formal / external / needs a paper trail** (invoices, contracts, customer confirmations) | **Email** | Searchable, forwardable, legally conventional |
| **Reference data / audit** (every event, every API response) | **Logged to a database** (Sheet, Notion, Postgres) — no notification | Queryable when needed, silent otherwise |
| **Errors and failures** | Dedicated `#alerts` channel, **deduplicated** | Separate from business noise so it stays trustworthy |

Three rules that come out of this:

1. **Every notification must have an owner and an action.** If nobody is expected to do anything, log it instead of sending it.
2. **Aggregate the routine.** Ten "new signup" pings is noise; one 9 a.m. message saying "10 new signups, 3 enterprise — full list here" is a briefing.
3. **Escalate rather than shout.** Send quietly first; only ping a human if it is still unhandled after N minutes.

##### Common pitfalls

- **Alerting on everything** — the muted-channel story.
- **Plain-text mentions** that never actually notify anyone.
- **Overusing `@channel`** until people leave the channel.
- **Ignoring rate limits** — Slack allows roughly one message per second per channel; Notion about three requests per second. Bursts get 429s.
- **Leaking secrets into messages** — a debug dump containing an API key is now in a searchable chat archive forever.
- **No deduplication on errors** — a failing loop can post the same alert 300 times.
- **Webhook URLs in public repos** — anyone can post to your channel.
- **Wrong Markdown flavour** — Slack's `mrkdwn` is not Discord's, is not Telegram's, is not standard Markdown.

##### Your hands-on tie-in

The practical task: set up a **Slack or Discord integration** and build an automation that posts a **nicely formatted message with a mention** to a channel when a trigger fires. Use Block Kit (or Discord embeds) rather than plain text, and resolve a real user ID so the mention actually pings. Compare the plain and formatted versions side by side — the difference in how "real" it feels is striking.

The mini project is a **daily standup helper**: collect updates from a Notion database or Google Sheet, format them into one summary message, and post it to Slack or Discord on a morning schedule. This is a genuine aggregation exercise — many records in, one message out — and it directly demonstrates the anti-fatigue principle.

For the assignment, write your **channel selection guidelines** covering email vs chat vs logged database, with concrete urgent and routine examples. Anchor each recommendation in the "owner and action" rule; that is what makes it advice rather than opinion.

##### Key takeaways

- Communication automation is a large share of real work, but the hard part is judgment about what deserves an interrupt.
- Slack offers simple incoming webhooks for posting and a bot-token API for everything else; Block Kit and correct `mrkdwn` make messages look professional.
- Discord embeds and Telegram bots cover community and mobile-first alerting cheaply; each has its own formatting quirks.
- Interactive buttons turn notifications into approvals — verify signatures and update the original message to prevent double-clicks.
- Match the channel to the urgency: mention for urgent, plain channel post for important, scheduled digest for routine, email for formal, silent log for reference.
